questions.q: What is assimilationist racism, as Kendi describes it?
a: Believing a group must change its culture to deserve equality
Believing one race is genetically superior to another
Refusing to discuss race in public life
Treating everyone the same regardless of history
questions.why: Lesson one defines it as the idea that Black people must adopt majority behavior before they can be treated equally.

questions.q: How did antiracists in the 1980s try to reduce violent crime?
a: By removing policies that kept young Black people unemployed
By demanding longer prison sentences
By increasing police patrols in neighborhoods
By funding more community sports programs
questions.why: Lesson one says they linked rising crime to Black youth unemployment and attacked the racist policies behind it.

questions.q: What does Kendi say about biological differences between races?
a: There are no meaningful genetic differences between races
Some races are naturally better at physical tasks
Race can be inherited but ethnicity cannot
Differences appear only in a few isolated traits
questions.why: Lesson two says humans are 99.9 percent genetically the same, and race is not something you inherit.

questions.q: Why does Kendi compare racism to his stage-four cancer?
a: Both have spread throughout the whole body or society
Both can be cured with a single treatment
Both are caused by poor personal choices
Both affect only a small part of the whole
questions.why: Lesson three says racism, like cancer, is present in every part of society rather than in one isolated place.

questions.q: What key difference does Kendi see between cancer patients and racists?
a: Patients accept their illness while racists deny theirs
Patients get support while racists are always punished
Patients can recover while racists never can
Patients seek help while racists usually hide at home
questions.why: The summary says cancer patients acknowledge the disease and fight it, whereas racists often remain in denial.
